source.title: Uncensored Is Not Unbiased: Abliteration Removes Refusals but Not Script-Dependent Bias About Taiwan

record.tranche_reason: Tests the practical weight-edit version of abliteration on released model pairs and measures refusals, but does not reproduce the original difference-in-means direction intervention or test it on harmful requests.
record.gate_note: The study reports refusal counts for political and historical open questions, not harmful requests. It does not estimate or ablate a refusal direction itself, add that direction, or test general capability as part of the refusal evaluation. Stance and control-country results are not rows for the tested version because they do not measure refusal removal.
record.test_reason: The study measures refusal counts before and after two released community abliterated builds, which bears on V2. The setting is new: political and historical questions (Taiwan, 1989) in three scripts rather than harmful requests. That makes it T3 rather than T2. No direction is estimated, ablated or added by the authors, so V1 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors conclude that abliteration removed every observed refusal in Qwen, plus part of the scripted PRC messaging, and moved its stance toward the ROC position. It did not remove the PRC position itself or the official 1989 names. In Bolt it barely changed stance and mainly increased acquiescence; refusal removal there cannot be shown because the original refused once in 243 answers. The script of the question mattered far more than abliteration: 'uncensored is not unbiased'.
record.recipe_differences: Uses community builds described as abliteration: a read-side projection for Bolt and a write-side edit for Qwen. The authors did not make either edit, estimate the directions, or verify that the edited values exactly implement the claimed direction removal; the Qwen tensors came from a third-party build.
record.method_sensitivity: Refusal counts are reported for different prompt sets and scripts. Qwen’s original 1989 refusal counts were 7/9 in Traditional Chinese, 7/9 in Simplified Chinese, and 9/9 in English; all were zero after abliteration. Bolt had only one refusal across all 243 open answers.

fits_no_version.finding: In Bolt, abliteration raised P(yes) on both statement sides (ROC side ~+0.1, PRC side ~+0.04) and in all 15 direct-question cells. The authors call this acquiescence, not a change of stance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-direction weight edits shift a general yes/compliance base rate on non-harmful yes/no questions.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen, abliteration raised Index S by +0.25 to +0.38 and reduced the scripted 'inalienable part' openings (166 to 115 answers). The model still affirmed 'Taiwan is part of the PRC' (P(yes) 0.77/0.98/0.80).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Abliteration removes refusals but not learned political assertions or stance.

fits_no_version.finding: Bolt's identity-deflection sentence in answer to the independence question (8 of 12 Chinese answers) persisted after abliteration. The authors say it behaves like a learned template, not a refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some deflection behaviours are not mediated by the refusal direction.

record.problems: The refusal evaluation uses only political and historical questions, not harmful requests. Bolt’s original build refused once in 243 answers, leaving little basis to assess removal. Only two model families and one community edit per family were tested; the authors did not create or recompute the edits. Qwen was evaluated by sampling, and the open-answer refusal measure is a mechanical classification.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant refusal results left out. Other reported results, including stance scores, script effects, corpus-marker frequencies, and steering outcomes, do not measure refusal removal for V2 and are not included as rows.

untested.parts: Refusal on harmful requests. General capability benchmarks beyond three control pairs and four general questions. Models beyond two community builds. Bolt: removal is untestable because the original almost never refused.
No difference-in-means direction estimated, ablated or added by the authors.

missing.what: Per-script total refusal counts for Qwen: original 7/9/10 of 81 (Traditional/Simplified/English), abliterated 0/0/0. Bolt original: 0/1/0.
Control-pair Index S before and after abliteration (e.g. Qwen 0.94/0.92/0.94 to 0.97/0.97/0.98). This is the only side-effect check on general judgment.

record.verdict_notes: The record's Bolt limits_scope label was dropped. A near-zero baseline makes the effect untestable, which belongs under untested and cannot_determine, not limits_scope. Neither edit was made or verified by the authors. Qwen evaluation used 20-sample estimates and a mechanical refusal-phrase classifier on the first 300 characters. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-versus-harmless activation-difference direction is estimated or ablated; no direction is added to induce refusals; the reported refusal evaluation uses political and historical questions, not harmful requests.
Tests two particular community weight-edited model pairs on political and historical questions, not refusal on harmful requests or a broad set of released models.
No jailbreak attack is tested and no training against ablation is performed.
Does not test whether refusal is carried by multiple directions, a cone, or an affine subspace.
Does not measure harmfulness judgments separately from refusal decisions.
Although the study tests political-question behavior across scripts and model pairs, it does not test transfer of a refusal direction across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct models.
Does not vary refusal-training data, method, or timing.
Thinking was disabled; reasoning models were not tested.

relation.reason: Its own before/after refusal counts on original and abliterated Qwen bear on whether released abliterated models stop refusing (V2).

tranche.reason: The study evaluates released abliterated builds on a new prompt domain (political and historical questions in three scripts, not harmful requests) and reports refusal counts before and after. It does not use the original method or measure (not T1/T2), and it reports a result on V2, so it is not T4.

source_check.notes: Only Qwen bears on V2. All four models are 2-bit, the refusal counts are mechanical phrase matches with no human coding, and the paper was run and drafted by an AI agent under the author's direction. The Qwen edit's tensors come from orcarouter's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored-GGUF; if the catalog's web:orcarouter source is that same release, the two are not independent.

statements.correction: arXiv:2610.29342: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, size not stated, ISTA-DASLab GSQ-RCO 2-bit (IQ2_XS) build. Edit: SC117 build whose 144 residual-writing tensors were copied from orcarouter's abliterated release; the authors did not recompute the values, and 89 tensors were re-stored at Q8_0. Refusals: 26/243 -> 0/243, counted as refusal phrases in the first 300 characters, 3 answers per question per script. 1989: 7/9, 7/9, 9/9 -> 0/9. Qwen control-pair Index S: +0.94/+0.92/+0.94 original, +0.97/+0.97/+0.98 abliterated. Capability evidence is only these control pairs; there are no CIs on the refusal counts. Bolt 74B-A9B is not usable for V2 (original refused 1/243).
statements.problem: The refusal numbers and control range are right for Qwen. But the condition '27B-70B models' is not in the text for this study: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's size is never given, and Bolt is 74B-A9B. The statement also leaves out that the builds are 2-bit, that the edit was unverified, and that refusals were counted mechanically.

statements.correction: Refusal here means refusal phrases in the first 300 characters of open answers. Four original-Qwen 1989 answers that gave the official narrative and declined details were not counted as refusals, and neither was Bolt's identity-sentence deflection (the authors say it is 'not like a refusal').
